mappings.note: Position, size and nature for one named object position in a concave mirror, read off the standard table rather than computed - LO-1's 'locates the image', not LO-2.
Value of c is asked only because refractive index is defined as c/v; it belongs with the refractive-index clause of LO-3 and nowhere else in this frame.
Speed of light varying with medium is the physical basis of refraction and of n - LO-3. Nothing here touches mirrors, formulae or diagrams.
Condition for no bending (normal incidence) is a direct consequence of the laws of refraction - the 'states the laws of refraction' clause.
Recall of n = c/v, i.e. the definition of refractive index. LO-3 is the only outcome that defines it.
Cause of refraction as change of speed - the explanatory half of the laws of refraction, not an application of the lens formula.
Interpreting n = 1.5 as a speed ratio tests the definition rather than any numeric substitution; still LO-3, which fuses definition and application.
Recall of 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. LO-3 says 'applies the lens formula'; this item only states it, but the frame offers no separate 'states the lens formula' outcome.
Whether a concave lens can ever form a real image - a standing property of the lens with no numbers and no formula, so the competency rather than LO-3, which is about applying the lens formula.
Direction of bending denser-to-rarer: the second law of refraction stated qualitatively.
Reciprocity of relative refractive indices - a property of the definition of n, which only LO-3 carries.
Absolute refractive index defined against vacuum; definitional, and LO-3 is the outcome that defines refractive index.
Emergent-ray/incident-ray relation for a slab stated in words; no diagram is required, so C 8.1-LO-2 is not in play.
Numeric relative refractive index, n(g,w) = ng/nw. This is substitution, but LO-3 fuses definition and application so it lands on the same code as the definitional items.
Defines magnification as the image/object size ratio - LO-2 is the only outcome naming the magnification formula. The item also covers lenses, for which no magnification outcome exists.
Names the concave-mirror property behind a shaving mirror (object inside F gives a magnified erect virtual image) - image characteristics by object position, LO-1.
Values of i and r at normal incidence, i.e. the law of reflection applied to a special case; the 'states the laws of reflection' clause.

A numeric substitution, f = R/2, rather than a qualitative image-location argument, so it goes with the quantitative mirror outcome even though LO-2's text names only the mirror and magnification formulae.

Two graded steps: drawing the slab ray path with angle of refraction and lateral shift marked, and computing the reciprocal refractive index. C 8.1-LO-2 is applied to a slab by extension - its text names only mirrors and lenses.
Completing the reflected path on a convex mirror is the ray-diagram outcome; marking i and r is the law of reflection (LO-1). No image is located and no formula is used.
Principal focus of a convex mirror defined by where reflected rays appear to come from - the virtual-focus idea LO-1 needs for convex mirrors.
Unit of lens power. Nearest legal code only - the dioptre appears in no outcome of this frame (defect list).
The one object position that makes a concave mirror image virtual - a straight image-location statement, no arithmetic.
Identifies the mirror from its invariant image characteristics (always virtual and diminished) - LO-1's convex-mirror clause.
Names the shaving mirror and gives magnification as the reason - still image characteristics by mirror type, not a computed magnification.
